title: Hadley–Godfrey reflecting quadrant (octant)
summary: Around 1731, Hadley and Godfrey independently developed reflecting quadrants that used paired mirrors to measure angular distances for navigation.

parents.reason: The Hadley reflecting quadrant mounted a sighting telescope so a navigator could align the directly viewed and reflected objects.

title: Campbell's lunar-distance observations with a Hadley quadrant
summary: Around 1747, John Campbell used a Hadley quadrant to measure the angular distance between the Moon and fixed stars, demonstrating the instrument in astronomical navigation.

parents.reason: The Hadley quadrant supplied the double-reflection instrument Campbell used to measure lunar distances at sea and at Greenwich.

title: Tobias Mayer's lunar tables
summary: Mayer's 1755 manuscript lunar tables predicted the Moon's position accurately enough to support longitude estimates at sea.

title: Campbell's sea trial of Mayer's lunar tables
summary: Campbell successfully tested Mayer's lunar tables and reflecting circle at sea, comparing them with the Hadley octant and recommending a more capable brass instrument.

parents.reason: The 1756 trial put Mayer's predicted lunar positions to navigational use aboard Campbell's ship.
Campbell directly compared the wooden Hadley octant with Mayer's heavier reflecting circle while measuring lunar distances at sea.

title: Nautical Almanac and Astronomical Ephemeris (1767 issue)
summary: The inaugural 1767 issue tabulated lunar distances and astronomical positions for mariners determining longitude at sea.

parents.reason: Mayer's accurate lunar tables supplied the predicted lunar positions used in early almanac longitude data.

title: Lunar-distance navigation with published almanac tables
summary: From the 1767 almanac issue, mariners could correct a sextant measurement between the Moon and another body, match it to predicted values for Greenwich time, and compare that time with local time to calculate longitude.

parents.reason: A sextant measured the lunar angle used to identify the corresponding predicted Greenwich time.
The almanac supplied predicted lunar distances and their Greenwich times for the observation date.
Clearing the observed angle for parallax and atmospheric refraction required spherical-trigonometric calculations.

title: Harrison's Jefferys precision watch (c. 1752–1753)
summary: Made for Harrison by John Jefferys around 1752–1753, the precision watch introduced temperature compensation and a miniature fusee that kept it running while wound.

title: Harrison H4 transatlantic trial
summary: H4 sailed aboard HMS Deptford from Portsmouth in November 1761; on reaching Kingston in 1762, its corrected timekeeping error corresponded to about one nautical mile of longitude.

parents.reason: The sea trial tested whether Harrison's H4 could retain reference time accurately enough to determine longitude across an ocean voyage.
The Board of Longitude arranged the Portsmouth-to-Jamaica trial that tested H4 at sea.
